---
title: "cloud infrastructure & scaling"
---

## what infrastructure supplies

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0"}

| component | definition | ml use case |
|---|---|---|
| compute | processors and memory used to run programs | train models or serve predictions |
| virtual machine | a software-defined computer with its own operating environment | host an inference service |
| gpu | a graphics processing unit, suited to highly parallel computation | accelerate suitable training or inference workloads |
| object storage | storage accessed as named objects through an interface | retain datasets, model artifacts, and reports |
| networking | connections and routing between systems | carry prediction requests and access inputs |
| load balancer | a component distributing requests across service instances | spread traffic across replicas |

:::

- choose resources from measured workload needs, including model memory, data access, and response time
- a managed endpoint is a provider-operated prediction service; use one when its operations and scaling features fit the workload

## tools and scaling terms

- infrastructure as code describes desired resources in versioned configuration; use it to review and repeat environment changes
- terraform is an infrastructure-as-code tool that plans and applies resource changes through provider plugins, which connect it to a platform’s api [terraform introduction](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/intro)
- docker compose defines and runs services on an existing docker host; use it for a small local environment [compose model](https://docs.docker.com/compose/intro/compose-application-model/)
- kubernetes coordinates containerised workloads across machines; a pod runs one or more related containers, while a deployment manages replicated pods and updates [deployment concepts](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/)
- vertical scaling increases resources for one instance; horizontal scaling adds instances, or replicas
- autoscaling adjusts replica counts or resources using configured signals; kubernetes’ horizontal pod autoscaler can adjust replica counts from observed metrics [autoscaling guide](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/autoscaling/horizontal-pod-autoscale/)

## aws building blocks

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0"}

| service | what it is | ml use case |
|---|---|---|
| s3 | object storage, organised into buckets and object keys | store raw data, versioned datasets, model artifacts, and reports |
| lambda | a serverless function that runs in response to an event, with no server to manage | lightweight glue logic — react to an s3 upload, validate a payload, trigger a pipeline |
| ec2 | a virtual machine you provision and manage yourself | run training jobs or services that need full control over the os and installed software |
| ecs | a managed service for running containers, on ec2 instances or on fargate (serverless containers) | run a containerised inference api or batch job without managing a container orchestrator yourself |
| sagemaker | a managed ml platform covering training, batch transform, and real-time endpoints | train and deploy models without assembling ec2/ecs/s3 plumbing by hand |

:::

- a bucket is a top-level s3 container; a key is an object's full path within it; enabling versioning on a bucket keeps every object revision instead of overwriting in place [s3 versioning](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/Versioning.html)
- ec2 and ecs sit at different points on the same tradeoff as kubernetes vs. a single host above: ec2 gives full control at the cost of managing everything yourself, ecs/fargate removes server management for containerised workloads, and sagemaker removes the deployment plumbing too, at the cost of less control over the serving stack
- default to ecs/fargate or sagemaker over raw ec2 unless something concrete requires direct os-level access — most training and serving workloads don't

## batch vs. real-time, on aws specifically

- sagemaker batch transform runs a model against a stored dataset and writes predictions back to s3 — the managed-service version of the [batch inference](../packaging-serving/serving.qmd) pattern, without provisioning and tearing down compute yourself [batch transform](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/batch-transform.html)
- a sagemaker real-time endpoint keeps a model loaded behind a managed http endpoint and auto-scales instance count with traffic; use it for the same case as [online inference](../packaging-serving/serving.qmd) generally — a caller needs a result back within the request
- a lambda function can serve a small model directly, without sagemaker, when cold-start latency (the delay before a fresh lambda instance is ready) is acceptable for the use case
- choosing between these is still the same question as batch vs. real-time anywhere: does a caller need this prediction back within one request, or can predictions be produced on a schedule and looked up later

## spark & databricks

- apache spark is a distributed data-processing engine; it partitions a dataset across a cluster so transformations run in parallel, useful once data no longer fits comfortably in memory on one machine [spark overview](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/)
- a spark dataframe looks similar to a pandas dataframe, but its operations are lazy — spark builds a plan and only executes it when an action such as writing output or counting rows is requested, rather than running each line eagerly
- databricks is a managed platform built around spark, adding a notebook environment, cluster management, and mlflow integration on top [databricks overview](https://docs.databricks.com/en/getting-started/overview.html)
- databricks ships mlflow natively, so the [experiment tracking](../experiments/tracking.qmd) and [model registry](../experiments/registry.qmd) patterns covered earlier work the same way there, pointed at a managed tracking server instead of a local sqlite file
- reach for spark or databricks once ingestion or feature engineering genuinely needs distributed processing; a dataset that fits comfortably in pandas on one machine doesn't need it, and adding it earlier than necessary trades simplicity for operational complexity with no benefit

## a local service configuration

- [download the deployment exercise](../../examples/deployment-demo.zip), which includes the earlier synthetic model and serving code
- prepare the model and image following the [packaging notes](../packaging-serving/containers.qmd), then use this `compose.yaml`

```yaml
services:
  api:
    image: ${DEMO_IMAGE:-mlops-demo:local}
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:${DEMO_PORT:-8000}:8000"
    cpus: 1.0
    mem_limit: 512m
    restart: "on-failure:3"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "python", "-c", "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:8000/health', timeout=2)"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 20s
```

- `DEMO_IMAGE` and `DEMO_PORT` are environment variables selecting the image and host port, with defaults after `:-`
- cpu and memory limits bound the container’s resources; these are example settings to measure and tune [resource limits](https://docs.docker.com/engine/containers/resource_constraints/)
- a health check periodically tests service state; this one checks the readiness endpoint after startup
- `on-failure:3` allows bounded restarts after unsuccessful process exits; an unhealthy check alone does not trigger this restart policy [restart behaviour](https://docs.docker.com/engine/containers/start-containers-automatically/)

```bash
docker compose config --quiet
docker compose up -d --wait
docker compose ps
```

- `config` validates the configuration; `up --wait` waits for services to run or become healthy where checks exist [compose up](https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/up/)
- one local container still depends on one host; replicas need independent failure capacity and suitable request routing
- each worker process may load its own model copy, so budget memory as well as cpu before adding workers [fastapi deployment concepts](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/deployment/concepts/)
